Bellman–Ford: relax every edge, |V|−1 times

1 / 5 Tip: the five thumbnails (a)–(e) under the graph are the textbook panels — click one to jump to that pass. Implement relax(u, v, w) not run 0 of 0 API (each call records a replay frame): dist(v) · setDist(v,val) · setPred(v,u) · weightOf(u,v) · note(text). plan.contextChunk: This figure contains five panels (a)–(e) tracing the execution of the Bellman-Ford algorithm on a directed weighted graph with five vertices s, t, x, y, and z and ten directed edges with weights 6, 7, 5, 8, −4, −2, −3, 9, 7, and 2. The same graph layout is used in all five panels: vertex s appears at the left, t and y in the center-left region, and x and z at the right; each vertex circle displays the current shortest-path estimate d[v] inside it. Panel (a) shows the initial state with d[s] = 0 and d[v] = ∞ for all other vertices, and all edges drawn as thin black arrows labeled with their weights. Panels (b) through (e) each show the graph after one additional relaxation pass; bold gray arrows highlight the edges whose relaxation improved a distance estimate in that pass, and updated d[v] values appear inside the affected vertex circles. After pass 1 (panel b), d[t] = 6 and d[y] = 7. After pass 2 (panel c), d[x] = 4 and d[z] = 2. After pass 3 (panel d), d[t] = 2 and d[z] = −2. Panel (e) shows the final shortest-path estimates d[s] = 0, d[t] = 2, d[x] = 4, d[y] = 7, d[z] = −2, with bold arrows forming the shortest-path tree along the path s → y → x → t → z. This figure demonstrates the Bellman-Ford algorithm's iterative relaxation process, showing how negative-weight edges cause distance estimates to decrease over successive passes until convergence.

interactionPlan.concept: Bellman-Ford finds shortest paths by relaxing every edge once per pass, repeating |V|−1 times so that estimates (including ones lowered by negative-weight edges) propagate outward and converge.
elements: Five vertices drawn as gray-filled circles with black outlines: s (far left), t (upper center-left), y (lower center-left), x (upper right), z (lower right)
Italic vertex name labels placed outside each circle: s left of its circle, t and x above, y and z below
Shortest-path estimate d[v] printed inside each circle (0, ∞, or a number such as 6, 7, 4, 2, −2)
Directed edge s→t with weight 6
Directed edge s→y with weight 7
Curved directed edge t→x with weight 5 (upper arc)
Curved directed edge x→t with weight −2 (lower arc of the same pair)
Directed edge t→y with weight 8 (vertical)
Directed edge t→z with weight −4 (diagonal down-right)
Directed edge y→x with weight −3 (diagonal up-right)
Directed edge y→z with weight 9 (horizontal bottom)
Directed edge z→x with weight 7 (vertical right)
Directed edge z→s with weight 2 (long horizontal back to s)
Numeric weight labels beside every edge, upright roman type
Bold gray highlight stroke drawn underneath edges that successfully relaxed in the current pass (predecessor edges)
Panel captions (a)–(e) in the static textbook version, corresponding to the initial state and the four relaxation passes
A pass counter / status readout showing the current pass number and how many distance estimates changed

interactions.teaches: That the entire Bellman-Ford algorithm is one tiny rule — relax(u,v,w) — applied blindly to every edge, pass after pass, and that the order of edges plus the guard condition determine exactly which estimates drop when.
interactions.label: Implement relax(u, v, w)

api.does: current shortest-path estimate d[v]; returns Infinity if not yet reached
update d[v] — the ONLY way to change a distance; records a frame and animates the number inside vertex v
record u as v's predecessor; shades edge u→v bold gray in the current pass
the weight w of edge u→v (also passed in as the third argument)
attach your own commentary to the current frame, shown in the replay caption

interactions.frame: the whole 5-vertex graph: every d[v] inside its circle, the edge just examined outlined, and edges whose relaxation succeeded shaded bold gray

input.label: Edge relaxation order (fixed, as in the textbook)

interactions.success_check: After 4 passes: d[s]=0, d[t]=2, d[x]=4, d[y]=7, d[z]=−2, and no further relaxation changes any estimate.

interactions.teaches: That each panel of the figure is exactly one complete sweep over all ten edges, and that the number of estimates that improve shrinks to zero as the algorithm converges.
interactions.label: Relaxation pass

interactions.teaches: That the bold gray edges are not just 'recently changed' edges but the predecessor pointers that together form the shortest-path tree rooted at s.
interactions.label: Highlight

demo_steps.title: Initialization (panel a)
demo_steps.narration: Every vertex starts at ∞ except the source s, which is 0. No edge is highlighted yet — the algorithm knows nothing but where it began.

demo_steps.title: Pass 1 — only s's neighbors can improve (panel b)
demo_steps.narration: Sweeping all ten edges, only edges leaving s find a finite dist(u), so d[t]=6 and d[y]=7. Two estimates changed; all the edges examined earlier in the order were useless because their tails were still ∞.

demo_steps.title: Pass 2 — the frontier advances (panel c)
demo_steps.narration: Now t and y are finite, so y→x gives d[x]=4 and t→z gives d[z]=2. Two more changes: information has travelled one more edge outward.

demo_steps.title: Pass 3 — negative edges pull estimates down (panel d)
demo_steps.narration: The negative edge x→t lowers d[t] from 6 to 2, which immediately lets t→z lower d[z] from 2 to −2. Estimates can go down, not just be filled in.

demo_steps.title: Pass 4 — convergence (panel e)
demo_steps.narration: A full sweep changes nothing: the counter reads 0. The bold edges now spell out the shortest-path tree s → y → x → t → z with final values 0, 7, 4, 2, −2.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: One dumb rule — 'if going through u is cheaper, take it' — applied to every edge |V|−1 times is enough, because after k passes every vertex reachable by a k-edge shortest path has its final value, and negative edges simply keep pushing estimates downward until nothing improves.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single graph panel (the demo replaces the five static panels a–e with one animated graph). Layout matches the textbook: s on the far left at mid-height; t upper-center-left and y lower-center-left forming a vertical pair; x upper-right and z lower-right forming a second vertical pair. Vertices are light-gray filled circles with thin black outlines, italic serif name labels outside (s left, t/x above, y/z below), and the current d[v] value centered inside in large roman type (∞ for unreached). Ten thin black arrowheads edges with roman weight labels: s→t (6) and s→y (7) fanning right from s; t→x and x→t drawn as a pair of shallow arcs between t and x, labelled 5 above and −2 below; t→y vertical (8); the two long crossing diagonals t→z (−4) and y→x (−3) forming an X in the middle-right; y→z horizontal along the bottom (9); z→x vertical on the right (7); z→s a long shallow arrow back to s (2). Relaxed/predecessor edges get a thick pale-gray stroke drawn underneath the black arrow, exactly as in the figure. Animate changing d[v] numbers with a brief flash. Beside the graph show a small readout: 'Pass k of 4 — n distances changed', plus a dist/pred table (s,t,x,y,z) updating live. Keep the code editor panel to one side with the fixed edge order listed above it so the learner can predict which relaxations will fire.

1 / 5 Implement relax(u, v, w) not run 0 of 0 API (each call records a replay frame): dist(v) · setDist(v,val) · setPred(v,u) · weightOf(u,v) · note(text). Goal: d[s]=0, d[t]=2, d[x]=4, d[y]=7, d[z]=−2 with no edge still relaxable.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Source is a 5-panel montage (a)–(e) shown side by side; the generated figure shows only one panel at a time via the step player / pass dropdown (acceptable design, but the on-canvas panel caption '(a)', '(b)', … present under each source panel is not drawn in the figure itself — only in the side-panel text).

In the source, all predecessor (tree) edges in a panel are shaded with the same heavy gray; the generated version renders edges relaxed in the current pass at full opacity and previously-set tree edges at 0.6 opacity, so panels (c)–(e) will not match the uniform shading of the original.

Minor label-position drift versus the source: the '2' (z→s) and '8' (t→y) weights sit slightly closer to the crossing lines than in the original, relying on white halos rather than the original's clear gaps.
Node value glyphs are slightly smaller relative to the circle than in the source (where the ∞ / digits nearly fill the node), making the figure read a touch lighter than the textbook art.
evaluation.notes: Accurate CLRS Bellman–Ford graph — correct vertices, all ten weighted directed edges with the right curved t↔x pair, correct arrowheads and gray node styling — with an unusually rich and pedagogically sound interaction set (pass stepper, narrated demo steps, tree toggle, sandboxed relax() workbench with replay); main shortcomings are the omitted on-canvas panel captions and the non-uniform (strong vs faint) tree-edge shading that departs from the source's single heavy gray highlight.
action_items: Draw the panel caption ('(a)', '(b)', …) beneath the graph so each step visually matches the corresponding source panel.

Render all predecessor-tree edges with the same heavy gray stroke as the source instead of splitting them into full-opacity vs 0.6-opacity classes (keep the distinction, if wanted, as a subtle optional overlay).
Nudge the '2' (z→s) and '8' (t→y) weight labels a few pixels further off their edges/crossings to match the source's clearer spacing.
Slightly increase the in-node value font so the numbers/∞ fill the circles as they do in the textbook figure.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interaction plan are sound (all 5s on concept/interactivity); remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes—missing on-canvas panel captions, non-uniform tree-edge shading, label nudges, and font sizing.

discrepancies: The source is a five-panel progression (a)–(e) shown side by side; the generated figure shows only one panel at a time behind a stepper/dropdown. This is a legitimate toggle implementation, but the at-a-glance comparison across passes that the original conveys is lost.

Edge-weight numerals are rendered noticeably smaller relative to the node values than in the source (17px vs 24px inside a ~480px-wide drawing), so weights like −2, −3, −4 read as secondary annotations rather than the prominent labels of the textbook figure.
Arrowheads are small solid triangles, whereas the source uses larger open/thin-stroked arrowheads; edge stroke weight is also lighter, giving a slightly thinner overall line look.

The '−2' label for the x→t arc sits very close to the arc itself (in the source it is clearly separated between the two arcs), and '−3'/'−4' sit in the crossing region between the t→z and y→x lines, slightly closer to the crossing than in the original.
evaluation.notes: Topologically exact reproduction of the CLRS Bellman–Ford figure (all 10 weighted directed edges, correct arcs, gray predecessor-tree highlighting, panel caption) with an excellent set of meaningful interactions — pass stepper, narrated demo steps, tree-focus toggle, d/π table, and a sandboxed relax() code workbench with replay — the main weaknesses being small weight-label typography and the loss of the side-by-side five-panel comparison.
action_items: Increase edge-weight label font size (to ~19–20px) and edge stroke width slightly so the weights match the visual prominence they have in the source panel.
Nudge the '−2' label further from the x→t arc and offset '−3'/'−4' away from the t→z / y→x crossing so no numeral touches an edge line.

plan.concept: Bellman-Ford finds shortest paths by relaxing every edge once per pass, repeating |V|−1 times so that estimates (including ones lowered by negative-weight edges) propagate outward and converge.
elements: Five vertices drawn as gray-filled circles with black outlines: s (far left), t (upper center-left), y (lower center-left), x (upper right), z (lower right)
Italic vertex name labels placed outside each circle: s left of its circle, t and x above, y and z below
Shortest-path estimate d[v] printed inside each circle (0, ∞, or a number such as 6, 7, 4, 2, −2)
Directed edge s→t with weight 6
Directed edge s→y with weight 7
Curved directed edge t→x with weight 5 (upper arc)
Curved directed edge x→t with weight −2 (lower arc of the same pair)
Directed edge t→y with weight 8 (vertical)
Directed edge t→z with weight −4 (diagonal down-right)
Directed edge y→x with weight −3 (diagonal up-right)
Directed edge y→z with weight 9 (horizontal bottom)
Directed edge z→x with weight 7 (vertical right)
Directed edge z→s with weight 2 (long horizontal back to s)
Numeric weight labels beside every edge, upright roman type
Bold gray highlight stroke drawn underneath edges that successfully relaxed in the current pass (predecessor edges)
Panel captions (a)–(e) in the static textbook version, corresponding to the initial state and the four relaxation passes
A pass counter / status readout showing the current pass number and how many distance estimates changed

interactions.teaches: That the entire Bellman-Ford algorithm is one tiny rule — relax(u,v,w) — applied blindly to every edge, pass after pass, and that the order of edges plus the guard condition determine exactly which estimates drop when.
interactions.label: Implement relax(u, v, w)

api.does: current shortest-path estimate d[v]; returns Infinity if not yet reached
update d[v] — the ONLY way to change a distance; records a frame and animates the number inside vertex v
record u as v's predecessor; shades edge u→v bold gray in the current pass
the weight w of edge u→v (also passed in as the third argument)
attach your own commentary to the current frame, shown in the replay caption

interactions.frame: the whole 5-vertex graph: every d[v] inside its circle, the edge just examined outlined, and edges whose relaxation succeeded shaded bold gray

input.label: Edge relaxation order (fixed, as in the textbook)

interactions.success_check: After 4 passes: d[s]=0, d[t]=2, d[x]=4, d[y]=7, d[z]=−2, and no further relaxation changes any estimate.

interactions.teaches: That each panel of the figure is exactly one complete sweep over all ten edges, and that the number of estimates that improve shrinks to zero as the algorithm converges.
interactions.label: Relaxation pass

interactions.teaches: That the bold gray edges are not just 'recently changed' edges but the predecessor pointers that together form the shortest-path tree rooted at s.
interactions.label: Highlight

demo_steps.title: Initialization (panel a)
demo_steps.narration: Every vertex starts at ∞ except the source s, which is 0. No edge is highlighted yet — the algorithm knows nothing but where it began.

demo_steps.title: Pass 1 — only s's neighbors can improve (panel b)
demo_steps.narration: Sweeping all ten edges, only edges leaving s find a finite dist(u), so d[t]=6 and d[y]=7. Two estimates changed; all the edges examined earlier in the order were useless because their tails were still ∞.

demo_steps.title: Pass 2 — the frontier advances (panel c)
demo_steps.narration: Now t and y are finite, so y→x gives d[x]=4 and t→z gives d[z]=2. Two more changes: information has travelled one more edge outward.

demo_steps.title: Pass 3 — negative edges pull estimates down (panel d)
demo_steps.narration: The negative edge x→t lowers d[t] from 6 to 2, which immediately lets t→z lower d[z] from 2 to −2. Estimates can go down, not just be filled in.

demo_steps.title: Pass 4 — convergence (panel e)
demo_steps.narration: A full sweep changes nothing: the counter reads 0. The bold edges now spell out the shortest-path tree s → y → x → t → z with final values 0, 7, 4, 2, −2.

plan.keyInsight: One dumb rule — 'if going through u is cheaper, take it' — applied to every edge |V|−1 times is enough, because after k passes every vertex reachable by a k-edge shortest path has its final value, and negative edges simply keep pushing estimates downward until nothing improves.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Single graph panel (the demo replaces the five static panels a–e with one animated graph). Layout matches the textbook: s on the far left at mid-height; t upper-center-left and y lower-center-left forming a vertical pair; x upper-right and z lower-right forming a second vertical pair. Vertices are light-gray filled circles with thin black outlines, italic serif name labels outside (s left, t/x above, y/z below), and the current d[v] value centered inside in large roman type (∞ for unreached). Ten thin black arrowheads edges with roman weight labels: s→t (6) and s→y (7) fanning right from s; t→x and x→t drawn as a pair of shallow arcs between t and x, labelled 5 above and −2 below; t→y vertical (8); the two long crossing diagonals t→z (−4) and y→x (−3) forming an X in the middle-right; y→z horizontal along the bottom (9); z→x vertical on the right (7); z→s a long shallow arrow back to s (2). Relaxed/predecessor edges get a thick pale-gray stroke drawn underneath the black arrow, exactly as in the figure. Animate changing d[v] numbers with a brief flash. Beside the graph show a small readout: 'Pass k of 4 — n distances changed', plus a dist/pred table (s,t,x,y,z) updating live. Keep the code editor panel to one side with the fixed edge order listed above it so the learner can predict which relaxations will fire.

discrepancies: The source shows all five panels (a)–(e) side by side; the generated figure shows one large panel plus a filmstrip of five thumbnails. The thumbnails carry the panel content, but their vertex values are rendered at ~6–8 px in the scaled group and are effectively unreadable, so the multi-panel comparison the source makes at a glance is lost.

In the thumbnails the heavy gray predecessor edges (the defining visual of panels b–e in the source) are drawn at ~2 px width and are barely distinguishable from the thin black edges, weakening the side-by-side progression.

Minor weight-label placement drift versus the source: the '−4' (t→z) and '2' (z→s) labels sit closer to the figure centre than in the original, and the white halo behind every weight (not present in the source) slightly lightens the crossing edges.
Vertex-value glyphs in the main panel are drawn at a slightly larger relative size than the source's, and the '(a)' caption sits nearer the graph than the generous caption gap in the textbook layout.
evaluation.notes: Structurally faithful CLRS Bellman–Ford graph with correct topology, weights, arc pairs, and a correctly simulated pass sequence (6/7 → x=4,z=2 → t=2 → z=−2), backed by unusually rich and pedagogically sound interactions (pass stepper, demo narration, tree focus, sandboxed relax() workbench with replay); main weaknesses are the illegibly small panel thumbnails that stand in for the source's five-panel composition and a few minor weight-label offsets.
action_items: Increase thumbnail scale (or reduce to 5 wider tiles) so the vertex distance values and the heavy gray predecessor edges are legible at inline size, since these encode the panel-to-panel progression of the source.
Bump the highlight stroke width in the thumbnails proportionally (currently HI_W*s ≈ 2 px) so tree edges read as 'bold gray' as in the textbook.
Nudge the '−4' and '2' weight labels outward along their edges to match the source placement, and reduce the white halo width so it does not visibly erase segments of the crossing edges.
Add a small always-visible legend note that thick gray = predecessor (shortest-path tree) edge, since the source relies on the reader inferring this from the panel sequence.
